articles.title: CVE-2026-62331: CVE-2026-62331: Path Traversal and Stored Instruction Injection in Praktor Telegram File Uploads
articles.description: CVE-2026-62331: Path Traversal and Stored Instruction Injection in Praktor Telegram File Uploads Vulnerability ID: CVE-2026-62331 CVSS Score: 8.2 Published: 2026-11-03 CVE-2026-62331 is a high-severity path traversal vulnerability (CWE-22) affecting Praktor versions prior to 0.9.1. Praktor is a multi-agent Claude Code orchestrator that integrates Telegram message handling with isolated Docker container workspaces. Due to improper sanitization of user-controlled filenames during Telegram document uploads, a remote user can escape the designated uploads directory and overwrite arbitrary files within the persistent agent workspace volume. Because the default configuration permits messages from any Telegram user without authentication, an attacker can overwrite critical agent instruction files such as CLAUDE.md, achieving persistent prompt and instruction injection across subsequent agent executions. TL;DR An unsanitized filename concatenation flaw in Praktor's Telegram upload handler (< 0.9.1) allows unauthenticated remote users to traverse out of the uploads/ directory and overwrite files in the persistent agent volume (/workspace/agent), resulting in stored instruction injection. ⚠️ Exploit Status: POC Technical Details Vulnerability Type: Path Traversal / Stored Instruction Injection (CWE-22) Affected Component: internal/telegram/bot.go & internal/container/manager.go Attack Vector: Network via Telegram Bot API Document Upload CVSS v3.1 Score: 8.2 HIGH (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N) EPSS Score: 0.78% (55.90th Percentile) Authentication Required: None (in default allow_from: [] configuration) Patched Version: Praktor v0.9.1 CISA KEV Status: Not Listed Affected Systems mtzanidakis/praktor praktor: < 0.9.1 (Fixed in: 0.9.1) Code Analysis Commit: c3731ee fix(security): prevent upload filename path traversal out of uploads/ (#228) diff --git a/internal/container/manager.go b/internal/container/manager.go index 1234567..89abcdef 100644 --- a/internal/container/manager.go +++ b/internal/container/manager.go @@ -577,8 +577,13 @@ func (m *Manager) WriteVolumeBytes(ctx context. Context, workspace, filePath stri var buf bytes. Buffer tw := tar. NewWriter(&buf) - targetPath := path. Join("/vol", filePath) - targetPath = strings. TrimPrefix(targetPath, "/") + // Defense-in-depth: reject any filePath that escapes /vol after path. Join + // collapses "../" sequences (e.g. a traversal-laden upload filename). + cleaned := path. Join("/vol", filePath) + if cleaned != "/vol" && !strings. HasPrefix(cleaned, "/vol/") { + return fmt. Errorf("invalid file path %q: escapes volume root", filePath) + } + targetPath := strings. TrimPrefix(cleaned, "/") parts := strings. Split(path. Dir(targetPath), "/") diff --git a/internal/telegram/bot.go b/internal/telegram/bot.go --- a/internal/telegram/bot.go +++ b/internal/telegram/bot.go @@ -425,7 +425,7 @@ func (b *Bot) processMediaGroup(ctx context. Context, msgs []telego. Message) { continue } - volumePath := fmt. Sprintf("uploads/%d_%s", time. Now().UnixNano(), att. Name) + volumePath := fmt. Sprintf("uploads/%d_%s", time. Now().UnixNano(), path. Base(att. Name)) containerPath := "/workspace/agent/" + volumePath if err := b.orch. WriteVolumeBytes(ctx, ag. Workspace, volumePath, data, image); err != nil { @@ -565,7 +565,7 @@ func (b *Bot) processMessage(ctx context. Context, msg telego. Message) { - volumePath := fmt. Sprintf("uploads/%d_%s", time. Now().Unix(), attachment. Name) + volumePath := fmt. Sprintf("uploads/%d_%s", time. Now().Unix(), path. Base(attachment. Name)) Exploit Details GitHub Advisory: Official vendor advisory detailing the path traversal mechanism and stored instruction injection via ../../../CLAUDE.md. Mitigation Strategies Upgrade Praktor to version 0.9.1 or later to enforce filename sanitization and volume root boundary checks. Configure explicit Telegram sender allowlists using the allow_from setting to block unauthenticated users from interacting with the bot. Audit existing persistent agent workspace volumes (praktor-wk-*) for unauthorized modifications to CLAUDE.md, skills, or hook files. Restrict agent tool permissions and MCP server access to minimize the post-exploitation impact of prompt or instruction injection. Remediation Steps: Stop the running Praktor orchestrator service. Update the Praktor binary or container image to release v0.9.1 (or build from commit c3731eeda01c0b3ec1dbd13cccd5a147c3182141). Edit the Praktor configuration file to specify trusted Telegram user IDs under the telegram.allow_from array rather than leaving it empty. Inspect the root directory of all persistent agent Docker volumes (/workspace/agent) to verify that CLAUDE.md and hidden configuration directories have not been tampered with. Restart the Praktor service and verify that file uploads are strictly written inside /workspace/agent/uploads/. References GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-48v2-6jcm-fc99 Official Fix Commit (c3731eeda01c0b3ec1dbd13cccd5a147c3182141) Praktor Pull Request #228 Praktor Release v0.9.1 NVD - CVE-2026-62331 CVE.org Record - CVE-2026-62331 CVEListV5 Repository Record Read the full report for CVE-2026-62331 on our website for more details including interactive diagrams and full exploit analysis.

articles.title: OpenAI Says ChatGPT’s Search-Like Query Volume Is About One-Fifth of Google’s
articles.description: OpenAI says ChatGPT’s web-search-like query volume is roughly 20% of Google’s traditional search volume, a ratio that puts the AI product’s discovery activity in clearer context while also exposing a major measurement problem for marketers. The figure comes from OpenAI product lead Adam Fry, who told Big Technology that ChatGPT’s search-like queries are about one-fifth of Google’s volume. However, the two numbers do not describe identical user actions. OpenAI counts a search whenever a person prompts ChatGPT to search the web, while conventional Google search-volume measures generally refer to queries submitted to a search results page. That distinction matters. Query activity can signal demand for information, but it does not by itself show whether users clicked through to publishers, ecommerce sites or business websites. For SEO and GEO planning, AI-assisted discovery should be measured alongside, rather than substituted for, traditional search visibility and referral data. What OpenAI said about ChatGPT search activity In Big Technology’s interview with Adam Fry, Fry described ChatGPT’s web-search-like query volume as approximately 20% of Google’s traditional search volume. In practical terms, that is the basis for the widely reported framing that Google processes about five times as much search activity. The statement is a useful first-hand indication of how OpenAI is thinking about search usage inside ChatGPT. It is not, however, an independently audited market-share figure. The interview does not fully disclose the geographic scope, the detailed counting methodology or how OpenAI separates web-search prompts from other ChatGPT interactions. ChatGPT has also been cited as handling roughly 2.5 billion prompts per day, or around 18 billion prompts per month. But prompts and searches are not synonymous. Many prompts ask for writing, analysis, coding or other assistance without requiring a web search. Conversely, a single research task may involve multiple conversational turns and web queries. Why a direct comparison with Google needs caution The key issue is definitional. A Google query generally begins a search-results-page session. A ChatGPT search-like query, under the definition Fry described, begins when a user asks the product to search the web. Both can reflect information-seeking behavior, but they occur in different interfaces and may lead to very different downstream actions. Measure What it represents Important limitation ChatGPT web-search-like queries Instances where a user prompts ChatGPT to search the web, under OpenAI’s stated counting approach. Does not necessarily represent a conventional SERP search or a visit to an external website. Google traditional search volume Queries submitted through Google Search. Volume alone does not reveal clicks, rankings, conversions or value by query. Website referral traffic Visits that arrive at a website from a referring platform. It measures outbound traffic, not all discovery or influence that happened within an answer interface. The distinction becomes especially important when discussions jump from query volume to claims about website traffic. Search Engine Journal’s recap of the interview notes that AI-assisted query counts and traditional referral traffic can differ substantially. Supporting analysis from Ahrefs illustrates the gap. Its representative-sample analysis reported Google at 24.74% of referral traffic and ChatGPT at 0.36%, and characterized Google as driving 190 times more traffic than ChatGPT in that analysis. Ahrefs also published a separate estimate that ChatGPT had 12% of Google’s search volume, underscoring that results can vary with definitions, datasets and counting methods. Read the methodology and findings in Ahrefs’ analysis of ChatGPT search volume. These figures should not be combined into a single market-share claim. OpenAI’s 20% statement concerns search-like activity, whereas Ahrefs’ referral figures concern outbound visits in a particular sample. A platform can answer a question, cite a brand or influence a decision without producing a click. Equally, high query activity does not guarantee meaningful traffic to a site. What this means for SEO and GEO measurement The most practical takeaway is to make the metric explicit before using it in planning or reporting. Teams comparing Google Search with ChatGPT should state whether they mean query volume, prompts, searches initiated, citations or referrals. Each answers a different question. For example: Traditional SEO reporting should continue to distinguish impressions, rankings, clicks and conversions in Google Search. AI visibility reporting can track whether a brand, product, source or page appears in relevant AI-generated answers, but that is not the same as receiving referral traffic. Discovery strategy should consider both pathways. A page may need to earn rankings and clicks in Google while also being understandable, well-supported and citable in AI-assisted experiences. This does not make traditional SEO less relevant. Google’s much larger query volume and referral contribution in the cited data reinforce the continuing importance of crawlability, indexation, helpful content and search-result performance. It does mean that reporting frameworks built only around blue-link clicks may miss some brand exposure occurring inside answer interfaces. Marketers should also avoid presenting ChatGPT’s reported one-fifth ratio as proof that AI search delivers one-fifth of Google’s website traffic, advertising value or commercial intent. None of those conclusions follow directly from the interview. The ratio is best understood as a directional indication that AI-assisted web discovery is significant, with comparability limits that need to remain visible. If you need a clearer way to assess where your site may be represented in AI-assisted discovery, create a GEO Search Leads account. It can help you assess website GEO readiness and identify optimization opportunities around content accessibility, entities and potential AI visibility. Use that assessment alongside Search Console, analytics and referral data so each channel is evaluated with the metric that actually fits it. Frequently Asked Questions Did OpenAI say ChatGPT has 20% of Google’s search volume? OpenAI product lead Adam Fry said ChatGPT’s web-search-like queries are roughly 20% of Google’s traditional search volume. The statement reflects OpenAI’s own counting approach, not an independently audited comparison of identical metrics. Why are ChatGPT prompts not the same as Google searches? ChatGPT prompts can cover many tasks, including writing, coding and analysis. OpenAI’s search-like measure counts instances where users prompt ChatGPT to search the web, while Google search volume generally refers to queries submitted to Google Search. Does one-fifth of Google’s query volume mean ChatGPT sends one-fifth as much website traffic? No. Query volume and referral traffic measure different outcomes. Ahrefs’ cited representative-sample analysis found a much wider gap in referrals, with Google accounting for 24.74% and ChatGPT for 0.36%. How should marketers compare AI discovery with organic search? Use separate measures for separate outcomes. Track Google impressions, clicks and conversions for SEO; assess citations, brand mentions and answer inclusion for AI visibility; and review referral traffic independently where it is available. Conclusion OpenAI’s one-fifth estimate is a meaningful signal about the scale of ChatGPT’s web-assisted activity, not a like-for-like replacement for Google search-volume or traffic data. Search teams should treat AI discovery as an additional measurement layer and define every comparison carefully, especially when translating visibility into expected visits or business results.

articles.title: Measuring AI Crawler Visits and AI Referrals on a Law Firm Site
articles.description: If you build or maintain websites for criminal defense firms, someone at the firm will eventually ask whether ChatGPT or Perplexity is sending them clients. It is a fair question, and the honest answer is usually "partly, and we can measure some of it." Two separate things are worth tracking: AI crawlers fetching the site, and people clicking through to the site from an AI answer. Neither measurement is perfect. Together they give a firm a far better picture than guessing, and they take a few hours to set up. This post covers the server-side and analytics-side pieces, with notes specific to law firm sites. Know which bots you are looking for The big AI providers each run more than one crawler, and they do different jobs. OpenAI documents GPTBot for collecting training data, OAI-SearchBot for ChatGPT's search features and ChatGPT-User for pages fetched when a person asks ChatGPT to look something up. Anthropic lists ClaudeBot for training, Claude-SearchBot for search quality and Claude-User for user-initiated fetches. Perplexity documents its own crawler as PerplexityBot. For a defense firm the search and user-initiated agents are the interesting ones. A visit from OAI-SearchBot or Claude-SearchBot suggests your pages are in the pool those tools can cite. A ChatGPT-User or Claude-User hit means a real person's question led the assistant to fetch your page right then. User agent strings can be faked. OpenAI publishes IP address lists for each of its crawlers as JSON files, linked from its bot documentation, so you can confirm that a request claiming to be OAI-SearchBot really came from OpenAI. Check the other providers' documentation for similar lists. Pull the visits from server or CDN logs JavaScript analytics will not see crawlers, since bots rarely execute your tracking script. You need raw access logs from the server, the host or the CDN. Many managed hosts let you download them, and most CDNs can export or query them. A quick first pass on a standard access log looks like this: grep -Eio "(GPTBot|OAI-SearchBot|ChatGPT-User|ClaudeBot|Claude-SearchBot|Claude-User|PerplexityBot)" access.log \ | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn That gives a count per agent. The next useful cut is which URLs each agent requested. On a law firm site, look at whether the search agents reach the charge pages, the attorney bios and the location pages, or whether they stop at the homepage. If they never reach the charge pages, check robots.txt, your CDN's bot settings and whether those pages are linked from anywhere crawlable. Run the count monthly and keep the results in a spreadsheet. Trends matter more than any single month. Capture AI referrals in analytics The second measurement is human visits that came from an AI tool. ChatGPT appends utm_source=chatgpt.com to many outbound links, which makes those sessions easy to spot in GA4 or any analytics tool that records UTM parameters. Other assistants mostly show up as referrals from their domains, such as perplexity.ai, claude.ai or gemini.google.com. In GA4, a custom channel group with a rule matching those sources gives the firm a single "AI assistants" line in its acquisition reports. Put the rule above the default Referral channel so the sessions land in the right group. Expect undercounting. Some app traffic arrives with no referrer at all and lands in Direct. Treat the AI channel as a floor, not a total. Tie it back to calls and forms A defense firm does not care about sessions. It cares about calls and consultation requests. Make sure the conversion events for phone clicks, form submissions and call tracking numbers are reported against the AI channel the same way they are for organic search and ads. If the firm uses a call tracking service with dynamic number insertion, check that it reads the source correctly for sessions tagged by AI tools. Then ask intake staff to record where each new client says they found the firm. A client who says "ChatGPT told me to call you" belongs in the report even if the session data never captured it. Remember what you cannot see Google's own AI features are harder to separate. Clicks from AI Overviews and AI Mode arrive from google.com and generally look like ordinary organic traffic in analytics. Google began rolling out a Search Console report for these features in 2026, described in coverage as impressions only and not yet available in every country. A firm can be named in an assistant's answer with no link click at all. Crawl logs and referral data show part of the picture, and a periodic manual check of what assistants say about the firm fills in some of the rest. For background on why some firms get named and others do not, this explainer on how AI assistants decide which defense lawyer to name covers the factors on the content side. Privacy notes for law firm sites Access logs include IP addresses and requested URLs. On a defense site, a URL path can hint at a visitor's legal trouble. Keep raw logs only as long as you need them, limit who can read them and avoid sending them to tools the firm has not approved. The firm's lawyers should decide the retention policy. More technical notes on AI search and legal marketing technology are collected in the ChatGPT and AI search technology library. Questions developers ask about AI traffic tracking Should we block training crawlers to save bandwidth? That is the firm's decision, not a technical one. Blocking GPTBot or ClaudeBot does not block the search agents, which use separate user agents. Why do AI referrals show up as Direct? Some apps open links without passing a referrer. The utm_source parameter that ChatGPT adds helps, but not every assistant adds one. How often should we review the logs? Monthly is enough for most firm sites. Look again after a site migration or robots.txt change. SBD Marketing works only with criminal defense firms, one firm per city. It builds websites for defense practices, handles SEO for the charges a firm defends, works on visibility in AI search tools and runs SEO audits.

articles.title: Deterministic Zero-Cloud Evaluation for AI Agents: Eliminating LLM-Judge Token Burn via Cryptographic Receipts
articles.description: How do you know if your autonomous AI agent is actually getting better? Today, the industry defaults to LLM-as-a-Judge (using GPT-4 to grade agent traces). But this approach has three critical flaws: Severe Token Waste: Evaluating 100 multi-turn agent runs burns $50+ in evaluation API calls. Non-Deterministic Flakiness: The judge LLM gives different grades to the identical agent output on different days due to model drift. Security Telemetry Leaks: Uploading agent trajectories to third-party evaluation clouds risks exposing sensitive customer data and private tool outputs. To solve this, we created agent-eval-harness — a 100% deterministic, zero-cloud evaluation engine for autonomous agents. Invariant Assertion Matrices & SHA-256 Merkle Receipts Instead of asking an LLM to subjectively "judge" an agent: State Invariant Assertions: Define formal criteria (e.g. required JSON schema, tool call sequence constraints, allowed latency bounds). Red-Team Leak Scanner: Deterministically scans agent outputs for unencrypted secrets, API keys, and SSRF private IP leaks. Cryptographic SHA-256 Merkle Receipts: Every evaluation produces an immutable cryptographic receipt verifying that test suite N passed on commit X. Hands-on Usage in Python Install via pip: pip install agent-eval-harness Evaluate an agent run: from agent_eval_harness import AgentEvalHarness, EvaluationSuite, AssertionRule harness = AgentEvalHarness.create_default() # Define formal evaluation criteria suite = EvaluationSuite( name="customer-support-agent-v1", rules=[ ] ) # Run evaluation on agent trace report = harness.evaluate_run( trace_path="./agent_trace_run_491.json", suite=suite print(f"Passed: {report.passed} ({report.score * 100:.1f}%)") print(f"Merkle Hash Receipt: {report.receipt_hash}") print(f"Zero Cloud API calls: $0.00 spent on LLM-judge tokens") Sovereign Ecosystem & Open Source ⭐ GitHub Repository: https://github.com/BenniAlencar/agent-eval-harness 🌐 Benni OS Portal: https://benni-os.net 📖 Full Architecture Article: https://benni-os.net/blog/

articles.title: I ran the same multi-agent experiment twice. Half the conclusions flipped.
articles.description: In August I ran a controlled experiment on my open-source multi-agent pipeline: the same task, done by 1, 4 or 6 agents, 30 runs each. The result was tidy. Four agents looked like the sweet spot: half the cost of six, and clearly better reports than one. In October I reran it with the same preregistered protocol on a different model. This time: Held: four agents were cheaper than six again, by more than before (60% fewer tokens, 54% lower cost, 49% less time). Flipped: "four agents write better reports than one" did not replicate. This time the single agent had the fewest problems. New: the reviewer agent in the six-agent arm failed its own output check on the first attempt in 27 of 30 runs. The cause was a limit that existed in the code's schema but not in the prompt. Adding one sentence to the prompt took the failures caused by that limit from 21 to 3. If I had published only the August run, this would be a neat "four agents is optimal" post. It doesn't hold on another model, so here are both runs. What the system does You give it a paper or a research topic, and it writes a commercialization screening report: scores for technology readiness (TRL), manufacturing readiness, patents and market, with a source cited for every claim. It is aimed at university tech-transfer offices, researchers and early-stage investors, and it produces a first-pass draft, not due diligence. It works in two stages. First, ordinary code retrieves papers, patents and market sources, validates and deduplicates them, and freezes them into a source registry. Then six LLM agents work only inside that registry: academic, patent and market analysts run in parallel, followed by a writer, a reviewer and a scorer. The weighted total score is computed by code, not by a model. The experiment Predictions before spending. Before any paid run, I committed the protocol, the decision rules and four predictions to the repository, so I couldn't move the goalposts after seeing results: Prediction P1 The four-agent writer passes the report-format check on the first attempt more often than the single agent P2 Six-agent reports have no more numbers that can't be matched to a source than four-agent reports P3 Going from six agents to four cuts cost and tokens by at least 20% P4 One agent is cheapest, but loses to four agents on at least one quality measure Three arms. A single "do-everything" agent that writes the report directly; four agents (three domain specialists plus a writer); and six agents, which is the full production pipeline with a reviewer and a scorer added. All three read the same frozen evidence and are held to the same report format and checks. Ten topics (from CAR-T cell therapy to room-temperature superconductors) × 3 repetitions × 3 arms = 90 runs, in Latin-square order. One caveat up front. The evidence was frozen in advance, so the experiment does no retrieval and calls no search API. The costs and timings below cover the model calls only and are much lower than a full production run. Only the six-agent arm has a scorer, so scores are not compared. Run 1: August, DeepSeek The 90 runs cost $1.80 and took about 2.7 hours. The main results: Six → four agents: compared topic by topic, 57% fewer tokens, 47% lower cost and 38% less time, with no quality loss. One → four agents: uncited claims fell from 115 to 24, at 2.4 times the cost. The reviewer barely edited. The final report kept a median 99.998% of the draft's text. A later blind comparison found that two evaluators each preferred the reviewed version in 7 of 9 pairs, so the reviewer wasn't useless; it just changed very little. P1 was wrong. The four-agent writer failed its first format check 5 times, the single agent once. Before the full study I spent under 6 cents on a pilot, which showed that the counter recording format-check failures was stuck at zero. The framework was calling a different entry point, so the counter was never attached. I fixed that before running the real thing. Why rerun it Two months later, production was on a different model and a lot of code had changed. I wanted to know whether August's conclusions survive a model change. So I wrote a second preregistration, with the four predictions and every decision rule copied unchanged, the same frozen evidence, and qwen3.8-flash as the model. To be clear, that is a small model chosen for its free quota, not the model production uses. Before the paid run I hit another problem: an offline check showed the experiment script would crash on start in the four- and six-agent arms. After August, the writer and reviewer prompt templates had gained new variables, and the script never passed them in. The fix was three lines, and it was found offline rather than by a paid run. The 90 runs recorded $0.64 at list-price upper bounds (about ¥3.4 actually charged, after the free quota) and took about 3.3 hours with no interruptions. Result 1: the savings held Four versus six agents, paired by topic: in August, 57% fewer tokens, 47% lower cost and 38% less time; in October, 60%, 54% and 49%. P3 held both times, and the savings grew. The six-agent arm also had a new problem: it completed only 23 of its 30 runs. More on that in Result 3. Result 2: the quality conclusion flipped In August, uncited claims were 115 for one agent, 24 for four and 38 for six: splitting the work clearly helped. In October they were 39, 166 and 115. Comparing report-format findings topic by topic, the single agent did better than four agents in 27 of 30 pairs. P4 was falsified, and P1 failed again (this time no arm failed a first attempt at all). There is a catch, which I found only after seeing the results. After August, the production writer template gained a "decision-output contract" section. It requires the report to state the assessment mode, the decision owner, the cost and time (or "not established"), and so on. Lines like these describe a mode or an absence, so there is nothing to cite, but the screen counts them as uncited claims. The four- and six-agent arms use today's template; the single agent still runs its frozen August prompt, which has no such section. Separating those lines out: 91 of the four-agent arm's 166 findings and 66 of the six-agent arm's 115 are contract lines. On all other lines the counts are 39, 75 and 49. The single agent still has the fewest, but the gap shrinks from more than 4× to under 2×. The rule for checking numbers also changed in September: figures in a unit the system can't recognize are now counted as unmatched. That makes this run's numeric check close to uninformative. So the reversal is partly the model, partly the template and partly the measuring stick itself, and I can't separate the three. Result 3: the sentence that wasn't in the prompt The six-agent arm completed only 23 runs because of the reviewer agent: in 27 of 30 runs its first output failed its own schema validation, and in 7 it still failed after a retry. By cause: Cause First attempt failed Still failed after retry A correction's reason longer than 300 characters 21 5 More than 20 corrections 0 Text to replace appears more than once in the draft 1 2 The reviewer prompt said "at most 20 corrections" and "find and replace text up to 2,000 characters", but never said "reasons up to 300 characters". That limit existed only in the code's data schema. So I preregistered a small follow-up: add only that sentence to the prompt, change nothing else, and rerun the same 30 six-agent runs ($0.36 recorded): First attempts failing on reason length: 21 → 3 First attempts failing for any reason: 27 → 6 Still failing after a retry: 7 → 2 Completed runs: 23 → 28 One side effect: the median number of corrections per review fell from 9 to 5.5. Whether the reviewer became more cautious, whether long reasons simply come with long edits, or whether it is day-to-day noise, this experiment can't tell. It also can't say whether fewer edits are better or worse. The same reviewer also behaved very differently on the two models. In August it barely changed anything; in October it made 241 corrections, and the final reports kept a median 99.17% of the draft text. (In production, a failed review falls back to the writer's draft, so the report still ships. But that is a paid review that changed nothing.) What these results don't show The differences can't be attributed to the number of agents. Between the two runs, the model, the provider, the writer template and both measurement scripts changed, across 669 commits. qwen3.8-flash is not the production model. Production was on qwen3.7-max-preview on October 23. These results say nothing about it. The prompts are asymmetric. The four- and six-agent arms run today's prompts; the single agent runs August's. Quality was screened by code only. The screens check whether claims are cited and whether numbers can be found in the sources. Nobody checked whether the reports are right, and the reviewer's edits were not judged one by one. The sample is small. Ten topics × 3 repetitions gives effect sizes, not statistical significance. Four lessons for anyone building agents Every constraint in your schema belongs in your prompt. One sentence took the failures from that limit from 21 to 3. When you rerun an experiment, lock more than the model. Lock the prompt templates and the measurement scripts too, or you won't know what changed the result. Spend a few cents checking your measuring instruments first. In August the pilot found a broken counter; in October an offline check found a script that would crash on start. Preregister, then publish both runs. Publishing only the run that flatters you is more misleading than publishing nothing. About the project GitHub: https://github.com/shuxiachai/academic-commercialization-agent Sample reports, no key or sign-up (five full assessments, one in Chinese): https://academic-commercialization-agent.up.railway.app/samples August protocol and results: https://github.com/shuxiachai/academic-commercialization-agent/blob/main/docs/prereg-2026-08-21-agent-topology-ablation.md October rerun results: https://github.com/shuxiachai/academic-commercialization-agent/blob/main/docs/results-2026-10-24-agent-topology-ablation-qwen.md One-sentence reviewer fix: https://github.com/shuxiachai/academic-commercialization-agent/blob/main/docs/results-2026-10-24-reviewer-reason-bound-qwen.md The protocols, results and limitations, failures included, are in the repository, along with the scripts that compute every number. The per-run output directories are not committed. Questions are welcome in GitHub Discussions, and the good first issues don't need an API key. I'd especially like feedback from people in tech transfer, research or early-stage investing: after reading a sample report, what is useful and what is wrong? And a question for other agent builders: how many agents does your pipeline have, and have you had a model ignore your output schema? How did you fix it? I'm Jingbo, a student at the University of Sydney. This post was drafted with AI assistance; every number was checked against the result documents linked above.

articles.title: Write Your Chrome MV3 Background Worker Like It Never Dies
articles.description: How a build-time AST transform finally makes Manifest V3 state persistence painless Manifest V3 didn’t just change the extension model — it actively punishes normal JavaScript patterns. Your background service worker is killed after roughly 30 seconds of inactivity. When Chrome restarts it, every top-level let, every Map, every pending setTimeout is gone. The next event handler starts from a clean slate. The official workaround is brutal: Manually serialize every piece of state to chrome.storage await it back on every event Rewrite long-running timers as chrome.alarms Maintain careful locking so concurrent restarts don’t cause duplicate work The result is hundreds of lines of defensive plumbing that has nothing to do with your actual feature. A different approach: transform the code, not the developer vite-mv3-sw-compile-persist takes a build-time approach. You keep writing ordinary JavaScript. The plugin rewrites your background entry so that state and timers actually survive restarts. You write: setTimeout(() => cleanup(), 5 * 60_000); After the transform you effectively get: Automatic dirty tracking on every mutation Restoration from chrome.storage.session (or local) on startup Long timers backed by chrome.alarms Recovery of registered callbacks after a worker death No runtime library to import. No decorators. No wrapper APIs. The source stays clean. How the transform actually works The plugin runs three passes over the background entry: 1. Analyze (Babel AST) It walks the AST and collects: Top-level let / var declarations (with special handling for Map, Set, Date, arrays, and plain objects) Every assignment and method call that mutates those variables All setTimeout / setInterval / clearTimeout / clearInterval calls Event handlers registered via .addListener Function declarations (needed for callback recovery) It is careful about control flow. Bare bodies of if / for / while are detected so the later injection of dirty-tracking code remains inside the correct branch. 2. Transform (magic-string) After every relevant assignment or mutation it injects __mv3_markDirty('varName'). When necessary it wraps the statement in braces first. Long timers (default threshold: 60 000 ms) are rewritten to __mv3_setTimeout / __mv3_setInterval wrappers that use chrome.alarms under the hood. Short timers stay native (with optional offscreen-document keepalive). Event handlers that do not return a value are made async and receive an await __mv3_init so restored state is guaranteed to be ready before your logic runs. Handlers that do return a value (classic onMessage return true, blocking webRequest, etc.) are left completely untouched. 3. Generate runtime A virtual module is emitted and inlined. It contains: State restore on startup Debounced flush of dirty variables (default 2 s) Serialization / deserialization for Map, Set, Date, and arrays Alarm registration and callback recovery via a function registry Stale-lock recovery for boolean flags (so an isRunning = true that never got cleared doesn’t deadlock the next incarnation) Optional Proxy-based reactivity when stateStrategy: 'proxy' is enabled The common path stays fast — almost nothing runs unless the worker actually restarts. Configuration that matters mv3Persistent({ backgroundEntry: /background[\\/]index\.ts$/, stateStrategy: 'proxy', // catch nested + Map/Set/Date mutations storageArea: 'session', // or 'local' alarmThresholdMs: 60_000, autoFlushMs: 2_000, keepaliveStrategy: 'alarm', // 'alarm' | 'offscreen' | 'none' staleLockThresholdMs: 30_000, promiseResolverStrategy: 'native', namedAlarmHandlers: { // for callbacks that can’t be auto-recovered cleanup: 'runCleanup', }, }) stateStrategy: 'static' is faster and sufficient for simple scalar / top-level reassignment patterns. proxy is the recommended setting for real applications that mutate objects, Maps, or Sets. What it deliberately does not break chrome.runtime.onMessage handlers that return true (or any value) stay synchronous. Blocking webRequest listeners are left alone. Source maps are preserved. The generated runtime is small and only activated on the restart path. Current limitations (honest list) Destructuring declarations (let { a, b } = …) are not supported for persistence — use individual lets. Anonymous timer callbacks that close over non-persisted local variables cannot be reliably recovered after a restart. Prefer named functions or register them via namedAlarmHandlers. new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, …)) is inherently fragile when the worker can die. The plugin warns and offers strategies, but there is no perfect solution. Requires Vite ≥ 8 and the "storage" (plus "alarms" when using long timers) permission. Why this approach feels different Most MV3 advice forces you to change how you write code. This plugin changes the compiled output so that ordinary code starts behaving correctly. The difference in day-to-day development is large: you stop thinking about the service-worker lifecycle on every line and start focusing on the feature again. If you maintain a non-trivial MV3 extension, try it on a side branch. The first time you kill the worker from chrome://serviceworker-internals and watch your counter keep incrementing, the value becomes obvious. Here’s the improved ending with a clear GitHub link and a proper call for stars: If you maintain a non-trivial MV3 extension, try it on a side branch. The first time you kill the worker from chrome://serviceworker-internals and watch your counter keep incrementing, the value becomes obvious. Try it Repository: https://github.com/GameGC/vite-mv3-sw-compile-persist If this plugin saves you from the MV3 state-management hell, please give it a ⭐. It really helps more people find it.

articles.title: BYD Sold More EVs Last Month Than the US Did All Quarter
articles.description: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Electrek: The world's leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company's highest monthly total in 2026. BYD's battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark. To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates. By the end of the year, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. "In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles," adds Electrek. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: How Neural Text-to-Speech Actually Works
articles.description: Introduction If you’ve ever played around with voice assistants, audiobooks, or AI‑generated podcasts, you’ve already experienced neural text‑to‑speech (TTS). What feels like magic on the surface is actually a cascade of deep‑learning models turning a string of characters into a natural‑sounding waveform. In this post we’ll peel back the layers, demystify the core components, and show you how to hook up a modern, production‑ready service—ElevenLabs—to your own projects. The Building Blocks of Neural TTS 1. Text Normalization Before any neural magic happens, the raw input must be normalized: Expand abbreviations (Dr. → Doctor) Convert numbers (123 → one hundred twenty‑three) Handle punctuation (determine pauses, intonation cues) Most open‑source pipelines ship a rule‑based normalizer, but recent models like Google's FastSpeech incorporate a learnable “text encoder” that can implicitly learn these patterns from data. 2. Phoneme Conversion Characters → phonemes (the smallest units of sound). This step removes orthographic ambiguity (e.g., “read” vs. “read”). A typical approach uses a grapheme‑to‑phoneme (G2P) model trained on a pronunciation dictionary. The output is a sequence like [DH, AH, N, EY, M, Z]. 3. Acoustic Modeling Here’s where the neural network really shines. Two popular families of models are: Seq2Seq with attention – Tacotron 2 maps phoneme embeddings to mel‑spectrogram frames. Non‑autoregressive – FastSpeech and VITS generate spectrograms in parallel, dramatically speeding up inference. The model learns to predict a mel‑spectrogram, a time‑frequency representation that captures the energy distribution across frequencies for each short time slice. 4. Vocoder A spectrogram is not audio; it’s a visual map. The vocoder converts that map into a raw waveform. State‑of‑the‑art vocoders include: WaveNet – Autoregressive, high quality, but slow. HiFi‑GAN – Generative adversarial network, fast and near‑real‑time. Vocoder in VITS – End‑to‑end models that merge acoustic modeling and vocoding into a single network. When you hear a synthetic voice that sounds like a human, you’re hearing the result of a spectrogram‑to‑waveform transformation performed by one of these vocoders. From Spectrograms to Waveforms – A Quick Walkthrough graph LR A[Raw Text] --> B[Normalization] B --> C[Phoneme Sequence] C --> D[Acoustic Model (e.g., Tacotron 2)] D --> E[Mel‑Spectrogram] E --> F[Vocoder (HiFi‑GAN / WaveNet)] F --> G[Audio Waveform] The diagram shows the data flow from raw text to the final audio signal. The crucial insight is that each stage can be swapped out or fine‑tuned independently, which is why voice cloning (customizing a model to sound like a specific person) is now accessible to developers. Voice Cloning & Fine‑Tuning Voice cloning essentially means adapting a pre‑trained TTS model to a new speaker’s timbre using a relatively small dataset (often just a few minutes of audio). The typical workflow: Collect a clean dataset – High‑quality recordings, consistent microphone, minimal background noise. Extract mel‑spectrograms – Using a library like librosa. Fine‑tune the acoustic model – Freeze the text encoder, train only the speaker embedding layers. Optional vocoder adaptation – If the target voice has unique spectral characteristics, a short vocoder fine‑tune can improve realism. Because the heavy lifting (the base model) is already trained on massive corpora, you can achieve impressive results with as little as 5‑10 minutes of speaker data. Getting Started with ElevenLabs – A Ready‑to‑Use API ElevenLabs offers a cloud‑hosted, high‑quality neural TTS service that abstracts away all the heavy training steps. Their API supports: Instant voice cloning – Upload a few seconds of reference audio. Real‑time streaming – Low latency for interactive apps. Fine‑grained control – Adjust speed, temperature, and voice stability. Below is a minimal Python example that sends text to the ElevenLabs API and saves the resulting audio file. import requests # Your ElevenLabs API key (keep it secret!) API_KEY = "YOUR_ELEVENLABS_API_KEY" BASE_URL = "https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1" def synthesize(text: str, voice_id: str = "default"): url = f"{BASE_URL}/text-to-speech/{voice_id}" headers = { "xi-api-key": API_KEY, "Content-Type": "application/json" } payload = { "text": text, "model_id": "eleven_monolingual_v1", "voice_settings": response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers) # The API returns raw wav bytes with open("output.wav", "wb") as f: print("Saved: output.wav") # Example usage synthesize( text="Neural text‑to‑speech has come a long way since the early days of concatenative synthesis.", voice_id="YOUR_CLONED_VOICE_ID" ) Curl Alternative If you prefer a quick curl test: curl -X POST "https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech/default" \ -H "xi-api-key: YOUR_ELEVENLABS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "text": "Hello, this is a demo of ElevenLabs TTS.", }' --output demo.wav Both snippets illustrate the core flow: text → API → audio. No need to manage spectrograms or vocoders yourself—ElevenLabs does it under the hood. Practical Tips for Developers Issue Why It Happens Quick Fix Mouth‑clicks or pops Vocoder mis‑alignment on very short pauses Add a tiny amount of silence () in SSML or increase the stability parameter. Pronunciation errors for rare words G2P model lacks coverage Use the SSML tag to force the correct phonemes. Latency spikes in real‑time apps Network round‑trip + server load Enable streaming mode (Accept: audio/mpeg) and cache the first 2 seconds locally. Cloned voice sounds “robotic” Insufficient speaker data or noisy recordings Record in a treated room, aim for at least 5 minutes of clean speech, and re‑upload. ElevenLabs also provides a dashboard where you can test variations of stability and similarity_boost in real time, which is a lifesaver when you’re fine‑tuning a clone. Where Neural TTS Is Headed Multilingual models – Unified architectures that can switch languages on the fly. Emotion control – Conditioning the acoustic model on affective embeddings (happy, sad, angry). Zero‑shot cloning – Generating a voice from just a few seconds of audio without explicit fine‑tuning. All of these trends rely on the same core pipeline we outlined, but with richer conditioning signals. As APIs mature, you’ll see more parameters exposed, letting you sculpt the voice just like a sound engineer. Conclusion Neural TTS is a layered system: text normalization → phoneme conversion → acoustic modeling → vocoding. Understanding each piece helps you troubleshoot, customize, and even build your own models if you’re feeling adventurous. For most developers, however, the fastest path to production‑grade speech is to leverage a hosted service. If you’re ready to experiment with high‑quality voice cloning, real‑time streaming, and fine‑grained voice control, give ElevenLabs a spin. Their API is straightforward, the documentation is solid, and the results sound remarkably human. Try ElevenLabs today: https://try.elevenlabs.io/kr07zfuqn1bp Happy coding, and may your apps speak as clearly as you think!
